---
title: "One food web and its 27 stability metrics"
author: "Simon Frost"
engine: julia
---

## Overview

The authors' simulation code is not public, so this package rebuilds it from SI §8–9 of
Domínguez-García et al. (2019). The published dataset is used to settle what the text leaves
open or gets wrong (see the project wiki: *Simulator reconstruction* and *Calibration*). This
vignette follows one community through the whole procedure:

1. draw a niche-model web;
2. run the bioenergetic model to a steady state;
3. compute the 27 metrics, from the Jacobian and from simulated presses and extinctions.

```{julia}
using EcologicalResilience
using DataFrames, Statistics, Random, Printf
using Plots
```

## A niche-model web

The niche model of Williams & Martinez (2000) places species on a niche axis and lets each
eat the species within a range below it. The connectance is 0.15, as in the paper.

```{julia}
rng = Xoshiro(42)
web = niche_model(rng, 30, 0.15)
L = trophic_levels(web)
(species = richness(web), connectance = round(connectance(web); digits = 3), basal = count(isbasal(web)),
 max_trophic_level = L === nothing ? missing : round(maximum(L); digits = 2))
```

## Assembly

`assemble_community` draws a web and the community's allometric exponents, starts from random
biomasses and integrates to a steady state. Species are removed when they fall below 10⁻⁶ of
their body mass. The web is discarded if more than 10% of its species die, and plants left
without consumers are then removed. Most draws are discarded. The `status` records why.

```{julia}
attempts = Symbol[]
c = nothing
while c === nothing
    global c, status = assemble_community(rng, 30)
    push!(attempts, status)
end
(attempts = attempts, initial = c.initial_richness, final = richness(c))
```

```{julia}
B = biomass(c)
alive = findall(c.model.alive)
scatter(c.model.trophic_level[alive], B; yscale = :log10, group = ifelse.(c.model.basal[alive], "plant", "animal"),
        xlabel = "trophic level", ylabel = "equilibrium biomass", size = (600, 380))
```

Without the metabolic loss that SI §8 lists for them, plants sit close to their carrying
capacity of 1. Only this choice reproduces the dataset's total biomass per plant (0.98).

## Responses to small pulses, from the Jacobian

The Jacobian at equilibrium gives resilience (the slowest return rate) and reactivity (the
fastest initial amplification). The amplification envelope A(t) = ‖exp(Jt)‖ is the largest
displacement at time t of any unit pulse. The "median" versions average over pulses
proportional to equilibrium biomass (Arnoldi et al. 2018).

```{julia}
J = jacobian(c.B, c.model)
C = pulse_covariance(B)
ts = 0:0.1:40
plot(ts, [amplification_envelope(J, t) for t in ts]; label = "A(t), worst pulse", lw = 2, yscale = :log10,
     xlabel = "time", ylabel = "displacement relative to the pulse", size = (600, 380))
plot!(ts, [median_displacement(J, C, t) for t in ts]; label = "median pulse", lw = 2)
```

```{julia}
Amax, tmax = max_amplification(J)
(resilience = resilience(J), reactivity = reactivity(J), Amax = Amax, tmax = tmax,
 median_reactivity = median_reactivity(J, C), stochastic_invariability = stochastic_invariability(J),
 sensitivity = press_sensitivity(J))
```

The equilibrium is reactive: some pulses grow by a factor of `Amax` before they decay. A pulse
spread over species in proportion to their biomass decays from the start.

## Responses to presses and extinctions, by simulation

Tolerance to mortality is the smallest increase in mortality that causes an extinction. It is
measured for all species at once (global) and for each species alone (local). Raising every
species' mortality by 10% and removing species one at a time give the resistance and
sensitivity metrics.

```{julia}
factors = 1.0:0.25:4
resp = [press_response(c, (m, _) -> set_mortality!(m, f)) for f in factors]
plot(factors, [100 * r[1] for r in resp]; lw = 2, label = "loss of total biomass (%)",
     xlabel = "mortality multiplier (all species)", size = (600, 380))
plot!(factors, [r[3] for r in resp]; lw = 2, label = "extinctions", seriestype = :steppost)
vline!([global_mortality_tolerance(c)]; label = "TM (first extinction)", ls = :dash)
```

`community_record` runs every experiment and returns the 39 raw columns of the authors'
Dataset S1. `prepare_metrics` then turns them into the 27 metrics, each signed so that larger
means more stable.

```{julia}
rec = community_record(rng, c)
m = prepare_metrics(DataFrame([rec]))
DataFrame(metric = METRICS, value = [m[1, k] for k in METRICS])
```
